canberra.title: Albo tells UK PM he’s changing the rules for British backpackers
canberra.snippet: The United Kingdom isn’t over the moon about Australia’s plan to change the rules for British backpackers coming to the country, bu...
canberra.content:
Anthony Albanese and Andy Burnham met on the sidelines at CHOGM. Photo: Anthony Albanese.

The United Kingdom isn’t over the moon about Australia’s plan to change the rules for British backpackers coming to the country, but both leaders have agreed to keep discussing “options”.

Anthony Albanese met with his UK counterpart, Andy Burnham, on the sidelines of the CHOGM meeting in the Caribbean this week, with both prime ministers discussing a range of issues important to each country.

On the backpacking issue, Mr Albanese said Mr Burnham engaged constructively with him on the matter.

The Australian PM said he put the case to the UK Prime Minister that the Federal Government aims to change the rules for backpackers to reduce Australia’s net overseas migration number.

Under the current free trade agreement with the UK, British backpackers can stay in Australia for up to three years without specific work having to be undertaken here.

Working Holiday Maker visas for other nationals require them to spend time working in regional areas if they want to extend their visas.

Australia is looking to extend that requirement to all backpackers.

Mr Burnham made no mention of that part of the conversation, and it was not included in the official readout of the bilateral meeting.

But Mr Albanese said the pair agreed to do more work on the issue.

“He [Mr Burnham] was very constructive about it, and we tasked our officials to do further work,” the Prime Minister told Australian journalists at CHOGM.

“There are options that we discussed. We’ll discuss it diplomatically. That’s how you get things done.”

About 77,000 UK nationals benefit from the current arrangement, but Mr Albanese said they’re not “benefiting from the experience of seeing the whole of Australia if they’re just staying in Sydney and Melbourne”.

“I advocated why I think change is necessary, and put forward several options, and we’ll work those issues through over the coming weeks.”

The PM didn’t offer a specific timeline or deadline for those options to be discussed further.

“The free trade agreement with the UK is overwhelmingly positive for both of our countries. This is something, though, that has had consequences in regional Australia that need to be accounted for, and that is why I’ve engaged in that way.”

Back in Australia, One Nation is insisting that British backpackers must work in regional areas to get extended visas.

One Nation MP David Farley said all backpackers should be required to work in regional locations if they want to stay in Australia longer than their initial visa allows.

“Now, if that was the case, we wouldn’t have them congregating around the Gold Coast and Bondi and Torquay and places like that,” he told ABC Radio National Breakfast on Wednesday (4 November).

“We’re paying the price of that now. We went from roughly 40,000 backpackers up to 80,000, literally holidaying for three years and turning themselves into coffee baristas.

“We need that workforce, and especially that age group of workforce, in regional Australia.”

canberra.title: Barr backs EU trade deal as tech and AI to step up to drive ACT growth
canberra.snippet: The adoption of artificial intelligence and continued development of technology-based industries will drive productivity and private sect...
canberra.content:
Chief Minister Andrew Barr: “There is no downside for the ACT in this agreement. It is one of the most important things we can do,”. Photos: Jasmine Thompson.

The adoption of artificial intelligence and continued development of technology-based industries will drive productivity and private sector growth in the ACT as migration and public infrastructure projects scale down, according to Chief Minister Andrew Barr.

In his State of the Territory speech at a Canberra Business Chamber event on Wednesday (4 November), Mr Barr also launched a staunch defence of the Australia-European Union Free Trade Agreement, which he said was vital for ACT tech firms to access that market.

Mr Barr said that after a decade of the country’s highest economic growth, the ACT would now need to pursue productivity gains through AI and play to its strengths in technology, cyber security, defence, education, health and renewable energy.

“It is clear how closely Canberra’s strengths in AI, cyber security, research and advanced technology align with the areas international investors are backing,” he said.

The Australia-European Union Free Trade Agreement would give Australian businesses access to a market of around 450 million people and a $30 trillion economy.

Mr Barr, who recently visited Germany and the UK, said researchers, engineers and technicians would benefit from an Innovation Mobility Pathway to travel, stay and work across the EU.

“Our universities and education providers will also have better access to the European market. For a city whose future depends on talent, research, services exports and international connections, the agreement presents a significant opportunity for Canberra businesses and workers,” he said.

Mr Barr said the agreement was an important opportunity to strengthen our trade relationships, attract investment and create new opportunities for Canberra’s knowledge-based industries.

“There is no downside for the ACT in this agreement. It is one of the most important things we can do,” he said.

“Imagine Australia turning its back on a trade agreement with the European Union. I’ve been Trade Minister for 15 years.

“I was there at the start of these negotiations. I’d like to be there at the finish and to see the real benefits that it will bring for our economy and for the Australian economy.”

Mr Barr says the ACT is a services exporter and technology services are the future.

Mr Barr said the government wanted more Canberra start-ups to succeed in global markets, attract more international investment, create more high-value jobs and increase the ACT’s exports.

“We want to turn more research into commercial success, attract talented people from around Australia and the world, and strengthen the industries where Canberra has genuine advantages.”

Mr Barr said no sector was better placed than the technology sector in terms of concentration of skills, talent and capital.

He told Region that much of the trade and commerce discussion focused on goods, but the ACT is not a goods exporter.

“We are a services exporter and technology services are the future, so undoubtedly that is a big opportunity,” Mr Barr said.

He said the success of Canberra companies such as Seeing Machines, Liquid Instruments and Quantum Brilliance showed the value of supporting a sector that was now maturing.

The energy transition was also giving Canberra an opportunity to develop expertise, technology and services that could be exported nationally and internationally.

The government’s Integrated Energy Plan was guiding the shift to an all-electric jurisdiction, while the Energy Innovation Fund was backing new ideas and positioning Canberra as an export-oriented hub for energy transition innovation.

Mr Barr said AI tools could make the ACT public service more productive without eliminating jobs.

He said they could help the workforce reduce processing times, improve customer interactions and free people to focus on more complex work.

“The objective is not a smaller public service. It is an increase in the output of the public sector,” he said.

“We want to use technology to deliver better services, make better use of public resources and improve productivity.”

Mr Barr said before his speech that it was important for humans to remain in the decision-making loop.

“But AI-assisted decision-making, particularly on things that are pretty black and white, it’s either eligible or it’s not against a set criteria, just being able to process all of those things more quickly will increase the output of the public sector,” he said.

Mr Barr said attracting talented people to the ACT and retaining them was also crucial to greater productivity.

He said the era of cheap money was over and that apart from Brisbane, where the Olympics would be held in 2032, all jurisdictions were winding back infrastructure spending.

In the ACT, the lyric theatre and the Convention and Entertainment Centre projects would deliver economic benefits, but the focus would turn to renewing ageing assets.

Whether some projects would need to be deferred was still on the table.

“We haven’t made any decisions to that effect yet, but we will need to see obviously the Commonwealth’s mid-year update, and their budget next year,” Mr Barr said.

He also said the ACT’s fiscal position had improved by about $100 million, according to the latest financial statements.

Net debt was $13 billion, but the Territory’s assets were now approaching $53 billion.

“So our balance sheet is in reasonable shape, but clearly an increased cost of capital in the near and medium term means you need to be prudent about projects that you’re borrowing for,” Mr Barr said.

He said the ACT was expected to pass half a million residents next year, and the economy would be worth $60 billion.

canberra.title: Independent public inquiry report finds AUKUS nuclear submarine ambitions are ‘unachievable’
canberra.snippet: A public inquiry into the trilateral AUKUS construct has released its Commissioner’s Report into one of Australia’s most controversial de...
canberra.content:
The public inquiry heard from more than 150 witnesses and 1000 submissions which overwhelmingly called for the AUKUS arrangement to be scrapped. Image: AUKUS, modified by Region.

A public inquiry into the trilateral AUKUS construct has released its Commissioner’s Report into one of Australia’s most controversial defence projects ever, the planned acquisition by the Royal Australian Navy of nuclear-powered attack submarines.

Titled Surrendering Australia, the AUKUS Deception, the report says the AUKUS Pillar I agreement between Australia, the UK and the US for nuclear submarines from these countries to be rotationally based in Western Australia from 2027, for Australia to buy up to five Virginia-class nuclear-powered submarines from the US in the 2030s, and for Australia to build new submarines of a British design in the 2040s should be scrapped.

The report says, since the AUKUS agreement was announced in 2021, the government has declined to thoroughly review the agreement, and hasn’t explained in detail how it advances Australia’s interests or better protects us.

“They have avoided answering fundamental questions about the costs and risks associated with AUKUS and have simply not answered the key question: ‘why AUKUS?’” it reads.

“Similarly, MPs from the major parties have brushed aside community concerns and avoided their responsibility to seriously debate in the parliament Australia’s largest ever defence acquisition program – estimated at over half a trillion dollars when the cost of nuclear waste disposal is included.

“After carefully considering all the material presented to us – over 10 days of hearings around Australia and more than 1000 submissions – we concluded that AUKUS is the worst, riskiest and most costly defence decision ever made by an Australian government,” it says.

“Neither the submissions we received nor the hearings we conducted uncovered any convincing foundations for AUKUS.”

The inquiry found the planned delivery schedule for the Virginia-class submarines and the follow-on SSN-AUKUS boats was “at best, problematic, and most likely unachievable”.

“What is more, successive governments have never adequately explained the need for nuclear-powered attack submarines in preference to submarine types with a more defensive capability and better suited to Australia’s regional waters.”

It said Australia had already spent about $9.2 billion to shore up the defence industrial bases of the US and UK and to start building a submarine shipyard in Australia, and that a further $50 billion was planned to be spent before any submarines are delivered.

“Extraordinarily, the lopsided agreement means the UK and US could walk away without delivering any submarines while retaining the billions of dollars we are providing to support their submarine building industries. Australia would have no redress,” it says.

AUKUS Inquiry commissioners former WA Labor premier and federal Labor minister Dr Carmen Lawrence, Yankunytjatjara woman Karina Lester, former Labor minister and Midnight Oil frontman Peter Garrett, former Chief of Navy and Chief of Defence Force Admiral Chris Barrie (Ret’d), and co-CEO of the Australia Institute Leanne Minshull. Image: Screenshot.

In addition to these doubts, the report also cited unexplained costs, a declining trust in government here and in the US and a growing overreliance on the US, questions over Australia’s sovereignty over the submarines, a lack of strategic justification premised on what it says are false assertions of an increased risk of war with China, and long-term high-level nuclear waster storage and disposal problems, as reasons not to proceed.

Coordinated by the Australian Peace and Security Forum (APSF) and funded through crowd sourcing, the inquiry was launched on 3 June with the goal of conducting open hearings into the proposed $368 billion project.

The inquiry was headed up by former Labor minister and Midnight Oil frontman Peter Garrett, and included fellow commissioners former WA Labor premier and federal Labor minister Dr Carmen Lawrence, former Chief of Navy and Chief of Defence Force Admiral Chris Barrie (Ret’d), the co-CEO of the Australia Institute Leanne Minshull, and Yankunytjatjara woman Karina Lester.

“This is a once in a generation, if not once in a century, serious level decision-making exercise by Australian governments plural,” Garrett said at the launch. “The Australian people need to be a part of it.”

Over the four months of the inquiry from June to September, hearings were held in Melbourne, Fremantle, Adelaide, Sydney, Newcastle, Wollongong, Brisbane, and Canberra. In total, the hearings heard from more than 150 witnesses, while more than 1000 written submissions were received.

“The Australian Peace and Security Forum, supported by several trade unions and community groups, combined to establish a public inquiry into AUKUS, relying on crowdfunding and grants,” the report reads.

“With terms of reference agreed, the inquiry accessed information available on the public record from the three AUKUS partners and invited submissions and testimony from experts and citizens.”

Presentations were made by former politicians including former prime minister Malcolm Turnbull, former Labor ministers for foreign affairs Professor Gareth Evans and Bob Carr, former Labor deputy prime minister and defence minister Kym Beazley, and former Coalition defence minister Christopher Pyne and defence industry minister Linda Reynolds.

Current politicians who presented included ACT independent Senator David Pocock, NSW Greens Senator David Shoebridge, and Tasmanian MP Andrew Wilkie, WA independent MLA Johanthan Huston, WA Greens MLC Sophie McNeill, SA Greens MLC Melanie Selwood, Newcastle Deputy Lord Mayor Charlotte McCabe and Greens Councillor for Newcastle Siobhan Isherwood.

“The government’s failure to appear and present comprehensive information on, and the reasons for, the AUKUS pact, and to answer the many serious questions asked by constituents was telling, and represents a failure in public accountability,” the report says.

Original Article published by Andrew McLaughlin on PS News.

canberra.title: High Court reinstates murder conviction for man who killed former partner
canberra.snippet: Michael O’Connell is potentially facing even more time behind bars after the ACT Director of Public Prosecutions successfully reins...
canberra.content:
4 November 2026

Michael O’Connell’s case will now return to the Court of Appeal after the High Court ruled that his murder conviction for the death of Danielle Jordan be reinstated. Photo: Facebook.

Michael O’Connell is potentially facing even more time behind bars after the ACT Director of Public Prosecutions successfully reinstated his murder conviction.

But he still may only be convicted of manslaughter.

O’Connell, now in his mid-40s, was originally found guilty of murdering his former partner Danielle Jordan (who was also known as Danielle Patricia Fleming) and sentenced to 15 years behind bars in 2024.

Ms Jordan suffered a serious head injury after being thrown from the bonnet of O’Connell’s ute in Melba on 15 April 2022. Her life support was turned off two days later.

In June 2025, the ACT’s Court of Appeal overturned that conviction and sentence, and in September of the same year he was found guilty of manslaughter.

He was re-sentenced in December 2025 to a backdated sentence of 10 years’ imprisonment, but the DPP launched an appeal to the High Court arguing the original finding of murder should be upheld.

On Wednesday (4 November), the High Court set aside the Court of Appeal’s ruling.

“The outcome of the DPP’s appeal is that the orders made in the first judgment will be set aside, Mr O’Connell’s conviction for murder will be restored [with a plea of not guilty],” it determined.

But O’Connell also had his own appeal submission to the High Court as part of the same proceedings.

It argued, in part, that even if the Court of Appeal could enter a verdict of guilty of manslaughter in the original decision, it had “erred in exercising that power”.

The High Court formally dismissed his submission.

“The proceedings will be remitted to the Court of Appeal to rehear Mr O’Connell’s appeal against his murder conviction,” it stated.

“It will be a matter for the Court of Appeal to determine what can and should be done in respect of the sentence subsequently imposed on Mr O’Connell for manslaughter.”

canberra.title: Five charged over alleged $235 million fraud activity against four Federal Government agencies
canberra.snippet: Five people have been charged across the country over an alleged $235 million racket targeting payments from the Education Department, Ve...
canberra.content:
Five people have been charged with fraud-related offences. Photo: AFP.

Five people have been charged across the country over an alleged $235 million racket targeting payments from the Education Department, Veterans’ Affairs, Services Australia, and the National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIA).

The arrests were made under Operation Integrity Fusion, a coordinated national blitz led by the Fraud Fusion Taskforce into entities suspected of submitting false claims for Commonwealth funds.

The sweep mobilised 108 police officers, along with 156 personnel from the affected agencies and the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission.

The activity was further supported by members of the police forces from NSW, Queensland, Victoria and South Australia.

Investigators seized 44 digital devices and 37 cloud-based accounts containing more than 28 terabytes of data from 26 search warrants across Adelaide, the Central Coast, Melbourne, rural Queensland and Sydney.

Investigators also confiscated more than $120,000 in cash, $15,000 in silver bullion, $11,000 in gold coins, and approximately $60,000 worth of jewellery.

Documents and other material relevant to ongoing investigations were also seized.

AFP Detective Acting Superintendent Stephen Raper said defrauding government agencies was a deliberate effort to take money that ultimately comes from the taxpayer.

“Service providers are there to support Australians who need it, and while the majority do the right thing, there are groups in our country who selfishly rort the system for their own personal gain,” he said.

“We continue to work with our partners in the Fraud Fusion Taskforce to stop targeted fraud which steals the money of honest and hard-working Australians and is a threat to Australia’s national security.

“Law enforcement and our partners will not stop in our pursuit of these people.”

The operation was coordinated in partnership with the whole-of-Australian Government Financial Crime and Money Laundering Working Group over three months.

Across seven investigations, authorities identified about $235 million in actual and potential fraud.

It is alleged that those charged defrauded government agencies by unlawfully obtaining personal or government-held information and claiming government-funded rebates and benefits for services that were either not provided or only partially delivered.

Investigations remain ongoing, and further arrests have not been ruled out.

Police dog investigating alleged government fraudsters. Photo: AFP.

NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commissioner Louise Glanville said providers who seek to exploit NDIS funding for personal gain should expect strong regulatory scrutiny.

“Fraud undermines the integrity of the NDIS and diverts funding away from its intended purpose, and the NDIS Commission remains focused on identifying and responding to serious provider misconduct wherever it occurs,” Commissioner Glanville said.

“Protecting the integrity of the NDIS requires a coordinated effort, and we will continue to identify, disrupt and take action against those seeking to misuse Scheme funding.”

An Education Department spokesperson said childcare subsidies are for those who need them.

“Ensuring providers correctly claim Child Care Subsidy protects the integrity of the early childhood education and care sector,” the spokesperson said.

“It ensures that the Child Care Subsidy is available for families with a genuine need for childcare. Anonymous tip-offs about childcare fraud can be made online via the Child Care Subsidy tip-off form.”

A Department of Veterans’ Affairs spokesperson said funding for veterans’ health and wellbeing was there to support those who have served our nation, not to be exploited for personal gain.

“The overwhelming majority of providers do the right thing; regrettably, some do not. Where we identify suspected fraud or serious non-compliance, DVA will act,” they said.

“Veterans and their families place their trust in providers to support them, and we will continue working with the AFP and our Fraud Fusion Taskforce partners to protect the integrity of the veteran support system.”

A Services Australia spokesperson said the work of the Fraud Fusion Taskforce not only helps agencies detect and disrupt serious fraud, but it also protects Australians.

“Through the Fraud Fusion Taskforce’s work, we’re disrupting scammers who attempt to steal people’s personal information to access their myGov accounts and commit fraud,” the spokesperson said.

australia.title: Endangered giant burrowing frog returns to wild after tadpoles rescued from ashes of black summer fires
australia.snippet: Tadpoles collected from puddles in East Gippsland were transported to Melbourne zoo, where they were raised to metamorphosis and successf...
australia.content:
After the 2019-20 black summer bushfires, scientists in eastern Victoria stumbled across something they had been after for years: puddles of tadpoles from the southern giant burrowing frog, one of the state’s most cryptic amphibians.

The fires had torn through extensive areas in East Gippsland, sparking concerns for the survival of the frog, which is considered critically endangered in Victoria.

About 160 tadpoles were collected and transported to Melbourne zoo, where they were raised through to metamorphosis into frogs and successfully bred in captivity for the first time last year.

In a homecoming more than half a decade in the making, 53 of the original tadpoles – now male frogs about five years old – have been returned to their native habitat in a remote area of the state’s east.

The elusive frogs grow to roughly the size of a cricket ball in adulthood, and are believed to have long lifespans. Matt Clancy, a herpetologist at Snowline Ecology and an expert in the species, said that like other large frog species such as green tree frogs, giant burrowing frogs “could quite easily get over 20 years old”.

“Being such a large frog, you think they’d be easy to find, but they spend a lot of time buried underground in … sandy soils and forested environments.

“They will hunker down and not move at all until the next rains come and they emerge,” he said.

The frogs surface to breed in ephemeral creeks and ponds only when conditions are right. Tadpoles can take three months to two years to metamorphose, usually emerging as juvenile frogs in spring or summer, Clancy said.

The 53 frogs were released immediately after big thunderstorms over the past several weeks at sites that had received 80 to 100mm of rain, he said.

Some of the released adults were not suitable for a captive breeding program run by Zoos Victoria. Ryan Moes, specialist amphibian keeper at Zoos Victoria, said the team conducted genetic testing on all the tadpoles originally collected.

“Within a breeding program, you don’t want to have all siblings breeding together,” he said. “The best thing to do was just to raise those frogs up and release them back out … into the wild once they were healthy frogs.”

Each frog was tagged before release, and song meters have been installed at release sites to detect the frogs’ calls.

Moes said the breeding program, which may involve future tadpole collections, ultimately aimed to ensure “those wild populations stay healthy and robust, and that the frog doesn’t go extinct”.

Giant burrowing frogs were split into two distinct subspecies – northern and southern – in 2021. Populations have been severely affected by habitat destruction and extreme climate events.

More frequent and severe bushfires and droughts due to climate change, as well as less rainfall, were ongoing existential threats, Moes said.

There are only five known breeding sites of southern giant burrowing frog in Victoria.

australia.title: Albanese government warned it’s ‘sleepwalking into another robodebt scenario’ over use of algorithms and AI
australia.snippet: Centre for Public Integrity report says mandatory audit and public register of all automated decision-making needed Get our breaking news...
australia.content:
The federal government is “sleepwalking its way into another robodebt” scandal amid a lack of transparency and legislation around use of algorithms and artificial intelligence in decisions, the chief executive of independent thinktank the Centre for Public Integrity said.

Dr Catherine Williams launched the centre’s “Computer Says No” report on Thursday, which examines the use of automated decision-making (ADM) tools by the government and calls for urgent reform.

The centre is concerned Australians may not know whether ADM has been used in decisions affecting them.

Among eight recommendations, the report calls for a mandatory audit and public register of all ADM use, and an independent oversight body with powers to monitor, audit and investigate the government over it.

Williams said the report was developed amid the centre’s increasing concern about the use of an algorithm as part of the government’s integrated assessment tool (IAT), which is used to assess the level of home support older Australians are entitled to.

The IAT has been found to be routinely under-assessing people’s needs and package entitlements, with aged care assessors banned by the government from overriding incorrect algorithmic decisions.

“We have been watching the evidence emerge in relation to the aged care algorithm tool, and becoming increasingly concerned about what is clearly the lack of an appropriate and robust framework to govern use of ADM by the government,” Williams said.

“It feels as though we are sleepwalking into another robodebt scenario, and that’s why we’ve decided to put this work forward now, in the hope also that it can help inform any framework that the government does propose in relation to ADM.”

The attorney general’s department has been developing an ADM framework, with public consultation ending in January 2025.

The attorney general, Michelle Rowland, did not respond to questions about when a draft framework might be complete and made public but said the government “is committed to ensuring the safe and responsible use of ADM to deliver timely and efficient services for the Australian community”.

The framework will implement recommendations from the royal commission into robodebt, she said.

A report from the commonwealth ombudsman, published in October, found transparency recommendations from the robodebt royal commission had been ignored by the government in developing and rolling out the IAT.

Rowland did not respond to questions about whether any ADM framework would be retrospective but said it “will be designed to improve accuracy and consistency of administrative decisions, embed robust safeguards, including transparency obligations, and ensure that ADM is used lawfully, responsibly, and with appropriate human oversight”.

The framework will also lift productivity and help deliver faster, more reliable services, she said.

In September, independent MP Kate Chaney introduced a private member’s bill to establish the first legislated, mandatory framework for ADM use by the government.

She said the attorney general department’s consultation process for an ADM framework “finished almost two years ago”.

“I have met with the attorney general about it and they say ‘We’re working on it’. I think it’s really important that we keep the pressure up so that it doesn’t get dropped because it’s too hard.”

Chaney said government departments are making decisions about ADM use with little consistency or transparency.

“The government wants to find cost savings in the public service and automating decision-making can be a way of achieving those savings,” she said.

“But I think trust in the government is low. There does need to be transparency about when decisions are automated, and when it’s not appropriate for those to be automated, for people to be able to get a clear understanding of why the decision was made and to be really clear about what the pathways are to review that decision.

“This is what people expect of government.”

australia.title: Australia has an especially bad inflation problem. So why are we only middle-of-the pack on the misery index?
australia.snippet: Comparing Australia to other countries may not be much comfort but does offer some perspective on the economy Get our breaking news email...
australia.content:
Is Australia’s inflation problem worse than the rest of the world’s?

A day after the Reserve Bank delivered its fifth interest rate hike for the year, increasingly stressed mortgage holders would be justified asking.

For Jonathan Kearns, the chief economist at Challenger, the answer is easy.

“Our inflation problem is worse than in other countries, that is very clear,” Kearns says.

The stats tell the story.

Consumer prices on average climbed by 4.3% in the year to September, and are anticipated to climb even faster by year’s end.

A quick survey of other advanced countries, and the eurozone, shows none with inflation near our level.

So far, so bad.

But before we break out the pitchforks, there is an important nuance that’s worth appreciating.

While our cost of living here is rising faster than in comparable countries, our labour market is stronger.

“Our performance in unemployment has been much better than in New Zealand, Canada and in Europe, and that is a positive thing for Australia,” Kearns says.

So should we be upset about having higher inflation than other countries, or relatively satisfied that our labour market has remained strong?

In other words: is the economic pain experienced greater here than in, say, New Zealand or Canada?

A very crude way of answering what is a complex question is the so-called “misery index”.

The concept was thought up by an American economist, Arthur Okun, in the 1970s – when it became popular enough to be weaponised during the 1976 presidential campaign.

The idea is simple: add the rates of unemployment and inflation together to create a very high level view of what households are experiencing.

By this measure, Australia goes from worst of the lot for inflation, to middle-of-the pack in overall misery.

That may not be much comfort, but it does provide some perspective to this challenging economic time we are living through.

australia.title: ‘Discontent and distrust’: annual social cohesion checkup shows exactly what’s making Australia angry
australia.snippet: Cost of living and AI outrank climate change and war as top concerns for future, but support for multiculturalism remains strong Get our ...
australia.content:
The vast majority of Australians support immigration and multiculturalism despite more feeling poorer – and increasingly pessimistic and distrustful of government, the annual Scanlon report on social cohesion has revealed.

People are more worried about artificial intelligence than climate change or going to war, but a global economic downturn and cost-of-living pressures are Australians’ key concerns.

Economic pain is also changing the way people vote, with people suffering hardship jumping ship to One Nation, according to the report, which is one of the country’s most extensive social research projects.

But, despite rising concern about antisemitism and Islamophobia, social cohesion in Australia has actually remained steady. The lead author of the report concedes many findings are cause for concern, but notes support for multiculturalism and diversity remains high, as does the sense of connection Australians feel to their communities.

“People are clearly under pressure with economic pressures, there’s discontent and distrust, people are blaming immigration … but we don’t necessarily see a permanence to that,” said Dr James O’Donnell from the Australian National University.

“It’s not just that people are getting angry generally. They’re really under pressure and that plays out in different ways.”

More than 10,000 Australians were asked 100 questions by the Scanlon Foundation on topics ranging from life satisfaction and financial circumstances to voting intent.

The report found happiness had declined most for millennials and generation Xers.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

The headline figure, the Scanlon index of social cohesion, remained at 78 out of 100 – a consistent figure since 2023.

The philanthropy organisation calculates this number through data about Australians’ sense of belonging, worth, social inclusion and justice, participation in society, and attitudes about acceptance.

“The really important stuff for social cohesion – the sense of belonging and acceptance – a lot of that is built into our daily life. There’s a resilience to that; we’re still volunteering, there’s a high level of trust in the people around us and local communities,” O’Donnell said.

But Scanlon concedes this headline number can “disguise” important shifts in individual numbers, including “increasing strain on Australia’s social cohesion”.

Despite the index remaining static, 62% of adults believe social cohesion has declined in recent years.

Australians pessimistic about their lives

Nearly one-third of respondents expect their lives to get worse over the next four years. That’s up from 29% last year.

While 79% of people said they had been happy in the past year – a number which has remained stable since 2021 – 48% said they were pessimistic about Australia’s future. That figure is up from 43% in 2025.

The Scanlon report said happiness had declined the most for millennials (born between 1981 and 1996) and gen X (born 1965-1980).

“Since 2014, the proportion of Millennials who are happy or very happy declined from 84% to 75%, while the proportion who are unhappy or very unhappy increased from 16% to 25%. Among Gen X, the proportion who are unhappy or very unhappy increased from 19% to 23%,” the report said.

“Across all generations, people are increasingly pessimistic about their future.”

Cost of living was by far the most-cited issue facing Australia, with 36% of people rating it as their top issue. Housing affordability and shortages was second on 11%, other economic issues on 10% and immigration on 9%.

On a different measure, about “major issues” facing the nation, 77% of Australians were concerned about a severe global economic downturn.

Scanlon warned many Australians were facing financial stress in ways which were “likely harmful to social cohesion”.

Some 20% of adults were unhappy with their financial situation. While 10% described themselves as “poor”, 13% said they had gone without food at least sometimes, and struggled to pay their rent or mortgage on time.

About one in five reported they sometimes had to go without medicine or healthcare, could not afford to heat or cool their homes, or had to ask friends or family to borrow money. Another 16% said they’d had to sell possessions because they needed cash.

Immigration and multiculturalism

While the social cohesion index remained steady, several key measures of cultural diversity have eroded.

Negative attitudes toward Indian immigrants rose to 33% in 2026, up from 25% in 2024.

In new questions asked in 2026, 36% of people said they had a negative attitude toward immigrants from Israel, 39% toward immigrants from Palestine and 41% toward those from Iran.

Some 18% reported a negative attitude toward Jewish people, up from 13% in 2024, while 43% said the same of Muslim people, up from 33% in 2024.

Negative attitudes to Hindus (17%, up from 13%) and Sikhs (20%, up from 14%) also rose since 2024, while negativity toward Christians dropped from 19% to 13%.

But public support for multiculturalism, despite a toxic political debate, remains very high. Some 87% of Australians believe immigrants are just as likely to be “good citizens” as Australian-born people, 76% agreed multiculturalism has been good for the nation and 73% agreed immigrants were good for the economy.

What is keeping Australians up at night?

After cost of living (36%), Australians’ top issues fell away quickly, to housing (11%), economic issues and immigration. The environment and climate change was the top issue for just 4% of people, with national security and terrorism at 1%, alongside health and education, social media, misinformation and artificial intelligence.

When asked about “major issues” facing Australia, 77% were concerned or very concerned about a global economic downturn. Despite only 1% rating it among their top issues, another 69% said they were worried about artificial intelligence – that ranked above climate change (55%) and a military conflict involving Australia (51%).

What does it mean for politics?

The report cross-references various figures with voting intention. It finds financial hardship may be contributing to support eroding for the Labor and Coalition parties, suggesting people feeling economic pain were more likely to vote One Nation or Greens.

This year, 42% of current Greens voters and 35% of those backing One Nation had gone without meals or healthcare, missed repayments, or couldn’t heat or cool their homes. That compared to only 24% of Labor voters and 23% of Coalition voters.

The Scanlon report found this is changing votes.

“Among people who voted for Labor or the Coalition at the 2025 federal election, we estimate that 47% who are experiencing financial hardship now prefer some other party or candidate compared with 36% of people who reported no hardship,” it said, with most of that vote shifting to One Nation.

In related findings, the report found that across all voting groups, “people experiencing financial stress are predicted to have substantially weaker trust in institutions”.

Political polarisation is also a feature of the report, with markedly different perceptions of society depending on voting intent. Only 9% of One Nation voters trust the federal government to do the right thing, and just one-third believe elections are fair and that courts make fair decisions.

That compares with 54% of Labor, 35% of Coalition and 25% of Greens voters trusting the government to do the right thing; 81% of Labor and 63% each of Greens and Coalition voters believing elections are fair; and 68% of Labor, 57% of Coalition and 54% of Greens voters believing courts make fair decisions.

Only 16% of Labor voters believe government leaders abuse their powers, compared to 64% of One Nation voters.

australia.title: Muslim Votes Matter softens anti-Labor stance ahead of Victorian election in bid to defeat One Nation in at-risk seats
australia.snippet: Exclusive: Advocacy group will put volunteers on the ground in Labor-held outer suburban seats that could swing towards Pauline Hanson’s ...
australia.content:
Muslim Votes Matter will relax its anti-Labor position at this month’s Victorian election, putting volunteers on the ground in key outer suburban seats the incumbent government risks losing to One Nation.

The grassroots advocacy group will direct its supporters to vote for Labor ahead of Pauline Hanson’s party in all lower house Victorian electorates and will aim to have volunteers on the ground in the seats of Greenvale, in Melbourne’s north, and Narre Warren South, in the city’s south-east, which the party fears could be seized by One Nation.

This is a departure from its position at last year’s federal election, where the pro-Palestine group focused on endorsing Greens and independent candidates to punish Labor, prompted by anger over the federal government’s handling of Israel’s war in Gaza.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Ghaith Krayem, the national spokesperson for MVM, said “circumstances have changed” ahead of the state election on 28 November.

But Krayem said the group would still not put Labor in the top spot in any seat on its how-to-vote cards, instead favouring independents and minor parties as it did at the 2025 federal election.

“As a community, we certainly don’t want to increase One Nation’s influence,” he said.

“There is a risk that if we went hard anti-Labor, like we did in the federal election, that would in fact benefit One Nation, and that’s not an outcome we want.”

Krayem said Muslim communities feared that if the Coalition was unable to form majority government, it could be forced to negotiate with One Nation and agree to some of its policy demands. He pointed to Hanson calling for a burqa ban in Australia as rhetoric that affected Muslim people.

“It becomes more normal for people to question the rights of how Muslims dress, to question the rights of whether the Muslim community is Australian enough,” he said.

“That is not a good place for the country or for the state.”

Krayem said MVM would preference Labor over the Liberal party in seats where preferences from the latter could flow to One Nation. The opposition leader, Jess Wilson, has been tight lipped when asked about preferences or potential deals with One Nation, saying the Coalition is running for majority government.

Greenvale, a seat created before the 2022 election and held by Labor on a 7.1% margin on a two-party preferred basis, has a significant Middle Eastern population.

“Given that it has a significant Muslim population, we think if we’re on the ground in Greenvale, we can shore up a bit of that support and minimise the risk of Greenvale becoming a One Nation seat,” Krayem said.

Labor holds Narre Warren South on a 8.3% two-party preferred margin and data from the 2021 census shows 13.1% of the constituency are Muslim compared to 4.2% state-wide.

MVM will also have volunteers on the ground in Tarneit, where 14.6% of residents in the electorate are Muslim. Labor holds the seat on a 12.3% margin.

Krayem said the outer western electorate was selected as a target seat following conversations with Muslim communities who said they were frustrated with Labor.

“Labor’s views with respect to Palestine, freedom of speech, protesting, all of those things, is still very much an issue across the community,” he said.

“Palestine and Gaza is still the number-one issue that our community is unhappy about at all levels of government.”

MVM will create how-to-vote cards for every lower and upper house seat based on how candidates align with its policy priorities, and volunteers will hand out the cards at polling booths in Greenvale, Narre Warren South and Tarneit. MVM’s Victorian policy priorities include tackling Islamophobia, cost of living and housing security, and respecting the rights of residents to advocate for Palestine.

world.title: ANC faces anger over poor services as South Africans vote in local elections
world.snippet: Party expected to get less than a third of the vote amid frustration over water outages and power cuts The African National Congress is o...
world.content:
The African National Congress is on course for a bruising result in South Africa’s local elections on Wednesday as voters go to the polls amid deep discontent over water outages, power cuts and crumbling infrastructure.

The former liberation movement, which Nelson Mandela led to power in 1994 at the end of apartheid as South Africa’s first black president, is still likely to be the largest party. However, polls showed it getting less than a third of the vote, down from 45.6% at the last municipal elections in 2021 and 40.2% in 2024’s national elections.

In Kensington, a diverse Johannesburg suburb that has sustained repeated water and power outages in recent weeks, voters said they wanted to see change. The city is currently led by Dada Morero, the ANC mayor, in coalition with the far-left Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF) and the rightwing populist Patriotic Alliance (PA).

“Service delivery is bad, it’s horrible,” said Tshepiso Makotse, 26, a call centre worker. “Water, electricity – everything, basically.”

Makotse said she had split her two votes, casting one for the centre-right Democratic Alliance (DA) local councillor and her party vote for the leftwing uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party of the former ANC president Jacob Zuma. “I just want change,” she said.

Terrence Pieters, a retired boilermaker, said: “The infrastructure in Johannesburg is shot.” He declined to say which party he had voted for, other than it was “one of the offshoots of the DA”.

“I would like to see things get better and great people in charge,” said the 72-year-old. “But … there’s no one party that’s going to take over here. It’s going to be a circus, it’s going to be a coalition.”

Vote fragmentation means the ANC could still end up leading many city coalition governments while losing control of others.

Unstable coalitions are already a feature of many of South Africa’s 257 municipalities, and analysts point to their high turnover as a major reason for poor service delivery.

Johannesburg, a city of 4.8 million people that has faced water shortages for more than a week, has had 10 mayors in as many years. The neighbouring municipality of Ekurhuleni has had three mayors since 2021. To the north, in Tshwane, which contains the capital, Pretoria, the mayoralty has rotated between parties four times since 2020. In October, more than 800 people contracted a gastrointestinal illness from contaminated water in Bronkhorstspruit, in east Tshwane.

The ANC’s national leadership is open to working with the DA in Gauteng, according to South African media, mirroring the government of national unity, where the two parties are the largest in the national coalition. However, local ANC leaders are reportedly not in favour of a DA tie-up. Currently, the ANC governs in various coalitions across the province’s three metros, including under an ActionSA mayor in Tshwane.

In Johannesburg, the DA’s Helen Zille has led a spirited campaign, with viral stunts including the 75-year-old snorkelling in a pothole and kayaking along a flooded street. However, the former Cape Town mayor is still viewed with suspicion by many, especially black voters, due to past comments appearing to excuse colonialism. Some voters also point to soaring housing costs in Cape Town, which has been run by the DA since 2006, as a reason not to vote for Zille.

The former Johannesburg DA mayor Herman Mashaba, who now leads ActionSA, which is polling around 10%, has ruled out working with Zille in Johannesburg. Mashaba has called Zille a “racist”, an allegation she has always fervently denied. The ANC, for its part, has three possible mayoral candidates for the city, amid factional infighting.

In eThekwini metro, which contains the port city of Durban, the MK party was polling above 40%. Zuma, its 84-year-old leader, who has weathered and denied numerous corruption allegations, is set to take many of the votes of his former party, which won 42% in eThekwini in 2021 and is now polling around 10%.

The DA looks set to retain its majority in Cape Town, although probably with less than the 58% of the vote it won in 2021, as unaffordable housing turns more voters against the party.

South Africa’s electoral commission will have a week to announce the final results of Wednesday’s vote, which chooses councillors and parties, with mayors not directly elected. Parties will then have two weeks from the announcement to form councils and elect mayors.

world.title: Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg
world.snippet: There is no end in sight for the drivers of illegal mining, while police action appears ineffective Cora Bailey has been encountering ill...
world.content:
Cora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991. But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area.

In late September, dozens of zama zamas – the name given to illegal miners in South Africa, meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare).

Soon, they were taking water for their panning and processing from the organisation’s two 25,000-litre water tanks, which are filled irregularly by the city government for the 100 or so rescued and injured animals on site.

“We’ve asked them really nicely and haven’t ever refused them water to drink … But, for the first time ever, we closed the gate at 12 [midday], because we literally had about two buckets of water left,” Bailey said in mid-October.

Police told her that the scale of the illegal mining was too big for them to do anything about, she said at the time. About a week later, officers sheared away the grass that had partly hidden the zama zamas. But within a few days a smaller group had returned, although Bailey said they were now taking Claw’s water only for drinking.

South Africa’s police regularly trumpet their success in tackling illegal mining. On 19 October, they said they had arrested 71 suspected zama zamas across the country in the previous week.

However, researchers put the number of illegal miners in the tens of thousands. In 2019, Marcena Hunter, a researcher at the Global Initiative against Transnational Organised Crime, estimated that a tenth of South Africa’s gold production, worth about $1bn, was being exported illegally.

Police operations have also led to tragedy. In 2025, 93 bodies were pulled from a mine shaft in Stilfontein, after officers blocked food and water from being delivered underground.

Meanwhile, there is no end in sight to the dynamics driving illegal mining, including the high price of gold, poverty, unemployment, corrupt politicians and police profiting, and the failure of mining companies to fulfil their legal obligation to seal mining shafts when they cease operating.

South Africa’s modern history is tied to mining. In 1884, gold was found on a farm, sparking a gold rush that led to the creation of Johannesburg. Gold production peaked in the 1970s, but South Africa was the world’s largest producer, a title it held for more than a century, until 2007.

In 2009, Morris Viljoen, a geology professor at the University of the Witwatersrand, estimated that the reef that gave the university its name had produced more than a third of the gold ever mined globally. Claw is housed in the old offices of the Durban Deep mine, which shut at the turn of the century, having once lent its name to an Elton John song.

The city government claims there is still 40,000 tonnes of gold underground in the region. But, with the remainder lying ever deeper, the costs of recovering it have risen.

Mining companies are supposed to seal up old mine shafts and rehabilitate the environment around them. However, in 2025 there were “6,100 derelict and ownerless mines and 1,170 unsafe mine openings”, the mining minister, Gwede Mantashe, said in response to a parliamentary question.

Zama zamas have stepped into those voids left in the earth. While there is no comprehensive data on them, experts agree that a majority are from neighbouring countries, principally Lesotho, Mozambique and Zimbabwe.

The skyline south of Johannesburg is punctuated by the pale yellow ridges of mine dumps. Increasingly, the ground is also caving open.

For politicians seeking votes in local elections on 4 November, the culprit is clear: illegal miners. In May, Kenny Kunene, the Johannesburg council member responsible for transport, took journalists on a tour of sinkholes that he claimed were the fault of zama zamas, including a section of Wemmer Pan Road that had completely collapsed.

The road was once the main artery linking the city’s central business district to the south-eastern suburbs. In one section it has completely disappeared, now raw earth pitted with the holes where illegal miners have been digging.

However, when it comes to sinkholes, experts say zama zamas are being scapegoated.

Rosalind Morris, an anthropology professor at Columbia University, who has worked extensively with illegal miners, noted that the porous dolomitic rock to Johannesburg’s south and west becomes unstable when water is removed.

“The biggest culprit of sinkholes in South Africa is formal industrial mining, which dewaters at a scale of hundreds of millions of gallons of water removed from underground every day,” she said.

“There are areas where there is a lot of residual gold, which are being very intensely mined by zama zamas, and some of that definitely causes structural collapse, there’s no doubt about it. But the idea that this was invented or caused for the first time by zama zamas is completely fallacious.”

Zama zamas are also frequently blamed for violence in mining areas, including a September mass shooting in Wedela township, west of Johannesburg. However, David van Wyk, the lead researcher at Bench Marks Foundation, said culpability laid with the often-feuding gangs that controlled access to the shafts.

“The guys working in the mine are actually super-exploited cheap labour … The guys with the guns are the guys who take the gold,” he said. “They don’t go underground.”

In Khutsong, about 50 miles (80km) west of Johannesburg, illegal miners, local and foreign, kept the township afloat, said Vusi Cele, the youth secretary for the local branch of Mining Affected Communities United in Action, a campaign group that advocates for “artisanal miners” to be granted mining licences. “Without those rents, it’s a ghost town,” he said.

While Cele, 33, currently hustles above ground selling mobile phone covers and screen protectors, he said he too would mine if he could get a licence. “On the surface there’s peanuts,” he said. “Underground there’s money.”

world.title: Sudanese diaspora and human rights groups denounce UAE nominee for UN top job
world.snippet: Critics cite Lana Nusseibeh’s denial of accusations the UAE is fuelling Sudan war by supporting paramilitary RSF Members of the Sudanese ...
world.content:
Members of the Sudanese diaspora and international human rights monitors have denounced the candidature of an Emirati diplomat for the top job at the UN, citing her denial of accusations that the United Arab Emirates is fuelling the war in Sudan by supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.

The UAE nominated Lana Nusseibeh last week to replace the UN secretary general, António Guterres, as he finishes his second five-year term ⁠this year, upending a race that had become gridlocked.

Rights groups and others have for years documented evidence of UAE support for the RSF, which has been accused of atrocities during the course of its war against the Sudanese army, including an attack on the city of El Fasher in October 2025 that the UN said had “hallmarks of genocide”.

Nusseibeh, the UAE’s representative to the UN until 2024, has repeatedly reflected the UAE’s blanket denials of the accusations.

The Sudanese pro-democracy and women’s rights activist Hala al-Karib, the regional director of the Strategic Initiative for Women in the Horn of Africa, said Nusseibeh had “no track record of acting independently of her country’s role in Sudan” and that endorsement by the security council would amount “essentially [to] a denial of the genocidal acts committed in El Fasher by the RSF”.

There was also strong criticism of Nusseibeh’s candidature at a virtual briefing by the Avaaz human rights advocacy group on Tuesday.

Ibrahim Alduma, who grew up in El Fasher and is the co-founder of the human rights organisation Sudan Action Hub, told the briefing that success for Nusseibeh would result in people losing faith in the UN.

“If this candidate [succeeds], how would we tell people on the ground that the United Nations is not an obstruction of the [rights of] the people of Sudan?” said Alduma. “How could the people – not only in Sudan, but other victims of wars and international criminals – trust that the UN will achieve some kind of justice?”

Husam Mahjoub, a Sudanese advocate and co-founder of independent media Sudan Bukra TV, said: “Electing [the UAE’s] senior diplomat as secretary general would hand leadership of (UN) institutions to that government’s chief defender, at the very moment Sudanese civilians most need the ‌UN to hold powerful states accountable.”

Kenneth Roth, a former executive director of Human Rights Watch, told the briefing: “She has been asked about the UAE’s role in arming and supporting the RSF, and she just blatantly denies it without regard to the facts. That is not what we need as UN secretary-general.”

On Wednesday, Bruno Stagno Ugarte, the chief advocacy officer at Human Rights Watch, said Nusseibeh’s dismissal of UN reports documenting the UAE’s links to the RSF had “seriously undermined justice and accountability for the victims”.

In a statement on Tuesday Nusseibeh said that if she got the top UN job she would support the work of UN fact-finding missions for accountability and transitional justice over the war in Sudan, and described the RSF’s crimes as “atrocious”.

She added that she had taken a leave of absence from her ministerial post in the UAE government to be “mindful of the obligations of independence” the UN role would entail, adding that “the horrific conflict in Sudan will be the litmus test of the success of an incoming secretary general”.

To become the next UN security general, a candidate must secure a minimum of nine affirmative votes out of the 15 security council members, and avoid a veto from the US, the UK, China, France or Russia, its permanent members.

An ​informal security council poll earlier his month had ‌placed the former Costa Rican vice-president ​Rebeca Grynspan as the narrow frontrunner in ​the race. But she and all other candidates received two or more opposing votes from the permanent council members. The next straw poll could take place as soon as Friday, but the format and exact timing are still being negotiated by the diplomats.

At Tuesday’s briefing, Roth said: “It’s fair to say the RSF would not have been able to be nearly as successful militarily as it was and has been without that support from the UAE. And with that support, it didn’t just fight the Sudan armed forces. This wasn’t just a civil war. It committed mass atrocities.”

He added: “It amazes me that she’s being put forward. This is a completely unsuitable candidate.”

Kate Ferguson, co-founder and co-executive director of Protection Approaches, a charity working to prevent identity-based violence, said at the briefing: “There is not, as far as I have seen, sufficient evidence that this candidate is independent from the state from which she comes. And we must not be naive nor hide behind the pretence of naivety.

“This is autocratic capture of our most significant multilateral institution.”

Additional reporting by Kaamil Ahmed

world.title: Egypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada Masr
world.snippet: Warnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed website Lina Attalah,...
world.content:
Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country.

Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt.

According to Mada Masr, Attalah was released after the news outlet had paid a fine of 3m Egyptian pounds ($53,500; £40,100), prompting statements of support from global human rights groups.

“Lina Attalah was released after we paid the said fine,” said her lawyer Hassan al-Azhari. “In the process, we discovered that she had been sentenced in absentia in 2024 to a year in prison, as well as a fine of 20,000 Egyptian pounds,” he told AFP.

Attalah’s defence team had appealed that sentence, and a new court hearing was scheduled for 11 November, Azhari added.

Attalah founded Mada Masr in 2013, after coming to international prominence in 2011 during the Arab spring. An advocate for press freedom, she has been arrested on a number of occasions.

Attalah’s detention, and the ordered closure of Mada Masr – which says it had applied for a licence to operate three years ago and had no reply from Egyptian authorities – follows the arrest of the entire six-person team at the independent factchecking platform Matsadaash, who were charged with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.

Attalah’s legal team suggested she had been, in effect, ambushed during a court appearance, with a judge appointing a defence lawyer for her before security personnel detained her in the courtroom.

The crackdown “can only mean that Egypt’s security agencies are moving from years of harassing independent media to wiping them out completely”, said Hossam Bahgat, the head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), who attended the court hearing.

“This escalation validates our fears that the arrest and continued detention of the six Matsadaash journalists would signal a crackdown of unprecedented magnitude,” said Bahgat. “It risks fully eviscerating the narrow margin of press freedoms that have been carefully maintained in Egypt over the past decade, albeit amid great personal sacrifice – a margin that had allowed the continued operation of a handful of news outlets and human rights organisations despite frequent harassment, including through legal avenues.”

According to EIPR, the recent moves against independent media follow an increasing frequency of statements from the Egyptian president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, since August claiming a conspiracy to destabilise the country. He has said he intended to remain in power until 2030 to protect Egypt from “traitors, criminals, and saboteurs”.

Reporters Without Borders said the court’s decision was “outrageous” and “shameful”, urging authorities to release Attalah “at once”. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) also condemned the verdict. Amnesty International said the verdict represented “a crushing blow to press freedom”.

Egypt is among the top jailers of journalists globally, with 25 currently behind bars, according to the CPJ. Attalah’s lawyers took steps to challenge the ruling, with a hearing in a retrial of the case scheduled for 11 November.

Underlining concerns over the crackdown, Pen International issued a statement with several dozen civil society organisations condemning the moves.

“Though this is the sixth case brought against Mada Masr in six years, this is the first time that a case of this nature has been referred to trial,” the writers’ association said. “For years, Egyptian authorities have leveraged their repressive and restrictive tactics against independent media outlets to harass journalists, restrict their operations and chill freedom of expression. To escalate to the step of referral to trial must be read as a clear intent to entirely shutter the independent media space, and to permanently close what remains.”

world.title: Africa’s ‘unprecedented’ Ebola outbreak could reach UK, says top health official
world.snippet: Jean Kaseya, of the Africa CDC, warns of the illness spreading like Covid unless more funding is secured to increase preparedness and pos...
world.content:
The “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak means it could reach the UK and other countries, according to one of Africa’s top health officials.

As the current outbreak reached 10,000 cases, with almost 5,000 deaths, Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), compared the outbreak to the Covid pandemic, which first took hold in China before spreading to countries across the world, claiming millions of lives, and ravaging health systems and economies.

“We want all countries to know that they are not safe if they don’t take appropriate measures,” he said.

“Each country, not only in the African region, but all continents, must now increase the preparedness level and the possibility for treatment.

“It is the first time three African regions have been affected [by Ebola]. The geographic extension of this outbreak is unprecedented,” he said.

Kaseya said leaders around the world should realise that although the brunt of the health crisis is affecting Africa at the moment, the situation could change. “We shouldn’t forget that at the beginning of Covid, many countries said there was zero risk of being affected, but a few months later, they became the hotspot,” he said. “We don’t want to see the UK and other countries become the hotspot.”

This outbreak, the 17th in the Democratic Republic of the Congo since Ebola was identified, was caused by the Bundibugyo virus and has become the largest and deadliest in the country’s history.

Ebola is a highly contagious, severe, and often fatal illness. It is spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies, such as during funeral preparations.

On 15 May, DR Congo’s health ministry declared an outbreak in Ituri province, though sequencing shows it had begun in February. It has now spread to Kenya and Uganda in east Africa, while last week, in west Africa, Nigeria confirmed a case in the capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus.

France is the only non-African country to have confirmed a case of Ebola so far – a doctor who had returned from DR Congo – in June.

The Bundibugyo virus has no approved treatment, though vaccine trials are under way. The results should be available in three to six months, said Kaseya.

Of the total 10,091 cases, 10,060 have occurred in DR Congo, with 4,887 deaths. Two people have died in Uganda, and two in Kenya.

The response to the crisis has been hampered by inadequate protective equipment and unpaid health worker wages, leading to strikes. Conflict in DR Congo as well as mistrust towards officials in affected areas, misinformation and global aid cuts have further complicated the situation.

Kaseya will convene a meeting of African health ministers on Wednesday to urge greater cross-border cooperation. He wants governments to introduce screening and testing for people coming from affected regions at points of entry and exit.

“The main message to ministers is that they have to understand they could be affected, and we don’t want them to be surprised by what could happen,” he said.

At a meeting in November with African heads of state, Kaseya will call for a “corridor of peace” in conflict areas. “Currently, we have colleagues in Ituri who want to go and support the population, but they cannot because of insecurity,” he said. “I have to say to leaders, this outbreak is not for rebels, it’s not for the official army, it’s for everyone. Ebola can affect everyone … We need to come together to have a kind of agreement on how to protect each other.”

Kaseya called for a global effort to fund the response. He said governments had pledged $3bn (£2.3bn), but that more than $2bn was still outstanding. African countries had committed $120m, he said, while the rest is meant to come from international donors including the US, the UK and the EU.

“We need this money now,” he said. “We must understand that failure to provide funding now to African countries [will result in more being spent] because the outbreak will continue to move. If we have other countries affected we’ll be talking about trillions of dollars because it will require a lot of support to stop this outbreak.”
